long.vo: For years, every T20 team had one. The anchor. The batter who stays till the end at a run a ball while everyone else swings. But in today's IPL, is the anchor dead?
The numbers say it should be. In twenty oh-eight, IPL top-order batters struck at one-thirty. By twenty twenty-five, it was over one fifty-eight.

So do the maths. Face forty balls at a strike rate of one-twenty, and you've cost your team fifteen runs compared with a typical top-order batter today. In a game decided by a few runs, that's the difference.

head.t: THE COST OF A SLOW INNINGS

long.vo: Now look at the ultimate anchor, विराट कोहली. In twenty twenty-five, he struck at about one forty-five. Then in twenty twenty-six, at thirty-seven years old, he struck at nearly one sixty-six, averaged over fifty-six, and RCB won back-to-back titles.
And in the final, chasing one fifty-six against Gujarat, he made seventy-five not out off just forty-two balls.

scene.label: OFF 42 BALLS · PLAYER OF THE MATCH
scene.note: RCB chase down 156 against Gujarat Titans

long.vo: So the role hasn't disappeared. It's evolved. The new anchor still bats deep, but at one fifty or more. He attacks the powerplay instead of waiting. He hunts matchups, picking the weakest bowler to target. And he doesn't leave the finish to someone else.

items.d: Time at the crease, without the cost
Picks the weakest bowler and goes after him
Doesn't leave the end to someone else

long.vo: Our verdict? The anchor isn't dead. The slow anchor is.
